fact: Often the first bird to sing in the morning, sometimes starting well before sunrise.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Lawns, parks, gardens and woodland edges, often running across grass and stopping to look down.
listen: A rich, rising and falling carol, often remembered as "cheerily, cheer-up, cheerio."
marks: Yellow bill and a broken white eye-ring

lookalikes.name: Eastern Towhee
lookalikes.tell: Orange only on the sides, with a white belly and a black or brown hood.

lookalikes.name: Varied Thrush
lookalikes.tell: In the West: an orange eyebrow and a dark band across the breast.

plumage: Females are paler, with a grayer head and duller breast. Young birds in summer have spotted breasts, a clue that robins are thrushes.
seasonNote: All year across most of the US, where winter flocks move into woods to eat berries. Summer only in Canada and Alaska.
nameNote: English settlers named it after the European Robin, which also has an orange breast, though the two aren't closely related. Turdus is Latin for thrush; migratorius means migratory.

fact: Unlike most songbirds, the female sings too, sometimes while sitting on the nest.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Thickets, gardens and woodland edges; often at feeders, early and late in the day.
listen: Loud, clear whistles that slur down and up, like "birdie, birdie, birdie" or "cheer, cheer, cheer."

lookalikes.name: Summer Tanager
lookalikes.tell: No crest and no black face, with a paler, thinner bill.

lookalikes.name: Pyrrhuloxia
lookalikes.tell: In the Southwest desert: gray with red trim and a stubby yellow bill.

plumage: Males are bright red all over. Females are warm tan with red on the crest, wings and tail. Young birds look like females but have a dark bill. Colors stay the same all year.
seasonNote: All year in the East and South, from southern Canada to Mexico. It doesn't migrate.
nameNote: Named for the red robes of Catholic cardinals. The scientific name says it twice: Cardinalis cardinalis.

fact: The more "dee" notes at the end of its call, the bigger the threat it has spotted.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Mixed and leafy woods, and backyards with trees, usually in small busy flocks.
listen: A sweet two-note whistle, "fee-bee," and the scolding "chick-a-dee-dee-dee."
marks: Gray back with white-edged wing feathers

lookalikes.name: Carolina Chickadee
lookalikes.tell: Nearly identical. It lives farther south, has less white on the wings, and sings four notes ("fee-bee, fee-bay") instead of two.

lookalikes.name: Mountain Chickadee
lookalikes.tell: In western mountains: a white eyebrow through the black cap.

plumage: Males, females and young all look alike, all year.
seasonNote: All year across the northern US and Canada. It doesn't migrate, and survives cold nights by letting its body temperature drop.
nameNote: Named for its call, "chick-a-dee-dee-dee." Poecile is Greek for many-colored; atricapillus is Latin for black-haired, for the cap.

fact: It can sing two notes at once, harmonizing with itself using the two sides of its voice box.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: The shady floor of mature leafy forests in summer.
listen: Flute-like phrases, often "ee-oh-lay," each ending in a soft, buzzy trill.
marks: Bold, round black spots on a white breast

lookalikes.name: Hermit Thrush
lookalikes.tell: Smaller spots, and a reddish tail that stands out from a browner back.

lookalikes.name: Brown Thrasher
lookalikes.tell: A much longer tail, streaks instead of spots, and yellow eyes.

plumage: Males and females look alike. Young birds have pale speckles on the back.
seasonNote: Summer only, late April to early October, in eastern forests. Winters in Central America.
nameNote: Wood for its forest home. Hylocichla is Greek for wood thrush; mustelina means weasel-colored, for its brown back.

fact: Each male knows several different songs and repeats one many times before switching.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Shrubby fields, marsh edges and yards, singing from a low, open perch.
listen: A few clear notes, then a jumble and a trill, remembered as "Maids, maids, maids, put on your tea kettle."
marks: Brown streaks that meet in a dark spot on the breast
Long, rounded tail it pumps in flight

lookalikes.name: Savannah Sparrow
lookalikes.tell: Shorter tail, a touch of yellow above the eye, and finer streaks.

lookalikes.name: Lincoln's Sparrow
lookalikes.tell: Finer, crisper streaks on a buff-washed breast, and a grayer face.

plumage: Males and females look alike. Color changes by region, from pale in the desert to dark and rusty in the Pacific Northwest.
seasonNote: All year across most of the US. Summer only in Canada and the northern Plains.
nameNote: Named for its song. Melospiza is Greek for song finch; melodia means melody.

fact: It weighs less than an ounce, yet its song carries across a whole neighborhood.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Tangles, brush piles and wooded backyards, usually low down and hard to see.
listen: A loud, rolling "teakettle, teakettle, teakettle."
marks: Rich rusty brown above, warm buff below

lookalikes.name: House Wren
lookalikes.tell: Plainer gray-brown, with no bold white eyebrow.

lookalikes.name: Bewick's Wren
lookalikes.tell: Grayer, with a long white-edged tail it flicks side to side.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year. Pairs stay together year-round and sometimes duet.
seasonNote: All year in the Southeast and East, and slowly spreading north. Hard winters knock northern numbers back.
nameNote: Named for the Carolinas, where it was first described. Thryothorus means reed-leaper; ludovicianus means from Louisiana.

fact: Its clear whistled song is often remembered as "Oh-sweet-Canada-Canada-Canada."
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Forest undergrowth in summer; brushy thickets and backyards in winter.
listen: A thin, pure whistle, "Oh-sweet-Canada-Canada-Canada."
marks: Yellow spot between the eye and bill
Striped head, black with white or tan

lookalikes.name: White-crowned Sparrow
lookalikes.tell: No white throat or yellow spot, a pink or yellow bill, and a cleaner gray breast.

plumage: Comes in two forms, white-striped and tan-striped, in both sexes. White-striped birds nearly always pair with tan-striped ones. Young birds have streaky breasts.
seasonNote: Winter in the eastern and southern US, October to April. Summers in Canadian forests.
nameNote: Named for its white throat. Zonotrichia means banded hair, for the head stripes; albicollis means white-necked.

fact: Every song opens with one long clear note, and each new song starts at a different pitch.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Conifer and mixed forests in summer; thickets in winter, often flicking its reddish tail.
listen: One long, clear note, then a spiral of airy flute notes; each song starts at a new pitch.
marks: Reddish tail that stands out from a browner back

lookalikes.name: Wood Thrush
lookalikes.tell: Bigger, bolder spots, and a rusty head rather than a rusty tail.

lookalikes.name: Swainson's Thrush
lookalikes.tell: Buff 'spectacles' and an even olive-brown back and tail.

plumage: Males and females look alike. Eastern birds are browner, western mountain birds grayer.
seasonNote: Winters in the southern US, October to April, and summers in northern and mountain forests. Elsewhere it passes through in April and October.
nameNote: Hermit for its shy, solitary habits. Catharus means pure, for its song; guttatus means spotted.

fact: It can imitate the scream of a Red-shouldered Hawk, possibly to warn other jays or scare off rivals.
size: Between a robin and a crow
habitat: Oak woods, parks and suburbs, often in noisy family groups.
listen: A loud, harsh "jay! jay!", soft bell-like notes, and hawk imitations.
marks: Black necklace on a gray-white chest
White bars and black stripes on blue wings

lookalikes.name: Steller's Jay
lookalikes.tell: In the West: a charcoal head and crest, and no white on the wings.

lookalikes.name: Eastern Bluebird
lookalikes.tell: Much smaller, with no crest and an orange breast.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year. The blue isn't pigment: it comes from light scattering inside the feather, so a crushed feather looks brown.
seasonNote: All year east of the Rockies. Some, not all, migrate in loose flocks along lakeshores in fall.
nameNote: Jay probably comes from its call or from the Latin gaius. Cyanocitta is Greek for blue chattering bird; cristata means crested.

fact: Its wings make a sharp whistling sound when it takes off, a built-in alarm for the rest of the flock.
size: Between a robin and a crow
habitat: Open country, farmland and suburbs; often on wires and at feeders.
listen: A soft, sad "coo-OO-oo, oo, oo."
marks: Slim body with a small round head
Long, pointed tail edged in white

lookalikes.name: Eurasian Collared-Dove
lookalikes.tell: Bulkier and paler, with a black half-collar and a square tail.

lookalikes.name: Rock Pigeon
lookalikes.tell: Chunkier, with a short fan tail and usually two black wing bars.

plumage: Males have a bluish crown and a pinkish chest; females are a little browner. Young birds look scaly.
seasonNote: All year across most of the US and Mexico. Summer only in the northern Plains and Canada.
nameNote: Named for its sad-sounding coo. Zenaida honors Princess Zénaïde Bonaparte; macroura means long-tailed.

fact: A male can learn around 200 songs, and unmated males often keep singing all night.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Towns, parks and open ground with shrubs, singing from rooftops and treetops.
listen: A long run of borrowed phrases, each repeated several times before it switches.
marks: Big white wing patches that flash in flight
Long tail with white outer edges

lookalikes.name: Loggerhead Shrike
lookalikes.tell: A black mask and a thick, hooked bill.

lookalikes.name: Gray Catbird
lookalikes.tell: Darker slate gray all over, with a black cap and a rusty patch under the tail.

plumage: Males and females look alike. Young birds have spotted breasts.
seasonNote: All year across the southern two-thirds of the US. It doesn't migrate.
nameNote: Named for its mimicry. Mimus polyglottos means many-tongued mimic.

fact: Males stuff sticks into several nest cavities, and the female picks which one to finish.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Yards, parks and woodland edges, often in nest boxes.
listen: A fast, bubbly cascade of notes that tumbles down the scale.
marks: Plain gray-brown, a little paler below
Fine black barring on the wings and tail

lookalikes.name: Carolina Wren
lookalikes.tell: Bigger and rustier, with a bold white eyebrow.

lookalikes.name: Winter Wren
lookalikes.tell: Darker and tinier, with a stubby tail, in deep forest.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year.
seasonNote: Summer across most of the US and southern Canada, April to September. Winters in the far South and Mexico.
nameNote: Named for nesting near houses, in boxes and odd spots like old boots. Troglodytes means cave-dweller; aedon is Greek for nightingale.

fact: It lines its nest with hair, sometimes plucked straight from a living animal.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Leafy woods and backyards with big trees; a regular at feeders.
listen: A clear, repeated whistle, "peter-peter-peter."

lookalikes.name: Black-crested Titmouse
lookalikes.tell: In Texas: a black crest.

lookalikes.name: Black-capped Chickadee
lookalikes.tell: No crest, with a black cap and bib.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year. Young birds sometimes stay and help their parents raise the next brood.
seasonNote: All year across the eastern US, slowly spreading north. It doesn't migrate.
nameNote: Titmouse is Old English: tit means small, and mase was an old word for a small bird. Baeolophus means small crest; bicolor means two-colored.

fact: It nests late in summer, waiting until thistles and milkweed have soft down for the nest.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Weedy fields, roadsides and feeders, in bouncing, roller-coaster flight.
listen: A twittering song, and a flight call like "po-ta-to-chip" with each dip.
marks: Black cap, and black wings with white bars

lookalikes.name: Yellow Warbler
lookalikes.tell: A thin, pointed bill, no black cap, and yellow wings.

lookalikes.name: Lesser Goldfinch
lookalikes.tell: In the West: a green back, and some males are black above.

plumage: Males are bright yellow with a black cap in summer, then turn dull olive-brown for winter. Females are olive-yellow with no cap. It's the only finch that molts its body feathers twice a year.
seasonNote: All year across much of the US. Summer only in Canada, winter only in the South.
nameNote: Named for its gold color. Spinus is Greek for a kind of finch; tristis means sad, oddly, for such a cheerful bird.

fact: A single male may have several females nesting in the patch of marsh he defends.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Marshes, wet ditches and fields, males calling from cattails.
listen: A gurgling "conk-la-ree!" that ends in a trill.
marks: Female streaky brown, like a big sparrow

lookalikes.name: Common Grackle
lookalikes.tell: Bigger and glossy purple-bronze, with a long keel-shaped tail and pale eyes.

lookalikes.name: Brown-headed Cowbird
lookalikes.tell: Smaller, with a brown head and a stubby bill.

plumage: Males are black with red and yellow shoulders they can hide or puff out. Females are streaky brown with a peachy throat. Young males look blotchy for their first year.
seasonNote: All year across most of the US. In the North it's summer only, and its arrival in March is one of the first signs of spring.
nameNote: Named for the male's red wing patch. Agelaius means flocking; phoeniceus means deep red.

fact: There is no blue pigment in its feathers: the color comes from how their structure scatters light.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Open fields and meadows with scattered trees, fence lines and nest boxes.
listen: A soft, warbling "tu-a-wee" or "cheer, cheerful charmer."

lookalikes.name: Indigo Bunting
lookalikes.tell: All blue, with no orange breast.

lookalikes.name: Western Bluebird
lookalikes.tell: In the West: a blue throat, and often rust on the back.

plumage: Males are bright blue above. Females are grayer, with blue on the wings and tail. Young birds are gray with spotted breasts.
seasonNote: All year across most of the East. Summer only in the North.
nameNote: Named for its color. Sialia comes from a Greek word for a kind of bird, and sialis repeats it.

fact: The female weaves a hanging pouch of a nest from plant fibers, hair and string.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Open woods, riversides and tall shade trees in parks and towns.
listen: Rich, flute-like whistled phrases, a little different from bird to bird.

lookalikes.name: Orchard Oriole
lookalikes.tell: Smaller, with deep chestnut instead of orange.

lookalikes.name: Bullock's Oriole
lookalikes.tell: In the West: an orange face with a black line through the eye.

plumage: Males are orange and black. Females are yellow-orange with grayish wings, sometimes with some black on the head. First-year males look like females.
seasonNote: Summer only in the East and Midwest, May to August. Winters from Mexico to northern South America, and in Florida.
nameNote: Named for Lord Baltimore, whose family colors were orange and black. Icterus is Greek for a yellow bird; galbula is a Latin name for a small yellow bird.

fact: Its song is often described as a robin that has taken voice lessons.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Leafy forest edges and wooded yards in summer.
listen: A sweet, robin-like caroling song, and a sharp "eek" call like a squeaky sneaker.
marks: Rose-red triangle on a white breast (male)

lookalikes.name: Black-headed Grosbeak
lookalikes.tell: In the West: the male is orange below instead of white and rose.

lookalikes.name: Purple Finch
lookalikes.tell: Females of both look streaky, but the grosbeak is much bigger, with a huge bill and a bold white eyebrow.

plumage: Males are black and white with a rose chest. Females are streaky brown with a bold white eyebrow, like an oversized sparrow. In fall, males turn browner.
seasonNote: Summer in northeastern forests, May to August. Winters in Central and South America.
nameNote: Grosbeak means big beak. Pheucticus means shy; ludovicianus means from Louisiana, where it passes through.

fact: One male was counted singing more than 20,000 songs in a single day.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: High in the leafy canopy of eastern forests in summer.
listen: Short phrases with pauses, over and over: "Here I am. Where are you? Over here."
marks: White eyebrow with a dark line above and below

lookalikes.name: Warbling Vireo
lookalikes.tell: A plainer face, no dark border on the eyebrow, and dark eyes.

lookalikes.name: Tennessee Warbler
lookalikes.tell: Smaller and greener, with a thinner bill.

plumage: Males and females look alike. Young birds have brown eyes.
seasonNote: Summer across eastern and northern forests, May to September. Winters in the Amazon.
nameNote: Vireo is Latin for I am green. Olivaceus means olive-colored.

fact: Its song is remembered as "drink-your-tea!", the last note a quick trill.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Brushy thickets and forest edges, scratching noisily in dead leaves.
listen: "Drink-your-tea!", and a rising "chwee?" call.

lookalikes.name: American Robin
lookalikes.tell: Orange across the whole breast, and no black hood.

lookalikes.name: Spotted Towhee
lookalikes.tell: In the West: white spots on the back and wings.

plumage: Males are black above; females are warm brown where the males are black. Young birds are streaky brown.
seasonNote: All year in the Southeast. Summer only in the Northeast and Midwest.
nameNote: Towhee comes from its call. Pipilo means I chirp; erythrophthalmus means red-eyed.

fact: It is named for its mewing call, which sounds remarkably like a cat.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Dense shrubs, hedges and tangled edges, often heard before seen.
listen: A long, rambling jumble of squeaks and whistles, with a cat-like "mew" call.

lookalikes.name: Northern Mockingbird
lookalikes.tell: Paler gray, with big white wing patches.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year.
seasonNote: Summer across most of the East, May to September. Winters along the Gulf Coast and in the Caribbean.
nameNote: Named for its cat-like mew. Dumetella means little thicket; carolinensis means from Carolina.

fact: It has been recorded with more than 1,100 different song types, usually sung in pairs.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Thickets, hedgerows and brushy edges, usually low down.
listen: Loud, varied phrases, usually sung in pairs: "plant-a-seed, plant-a-seed."
marks: Rusty back and very long tail
Bold brown streaks on a white breast
Yellow eyes and a long, curved bill

lookalikes.name: Wood Thrush
lookalikes.tell: Shorter tail, round spots and dark eyes.

lookalikes.name: Long-billed Thrasher
lookalikes.tell: In south Texas: a grayer face and a longer bill.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year.
seasonNote: All year in the Southeast. Summer only in the North and on the Plains, April to October.
nameNote: Thrasher may come from thrusher, an old word for thrush, or from the way it thrashes through dead leaves. Toxostoma means bow-mouthed; rufum means reddish.

fact: It is the state bird of six US states, more than almost any other bird.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Grasslands, prairies and farm fields, singing from fence posts.
listen: A bubbling, flute-like song that tumbles down at the end.
marks: Streaky brown back and white outer tail feathers

lookalikes.name: Eastern Meadowlark
lookalikes.tell: Nearly identical; tell them by song. The Eastern's is a few simple, slurred whistles.

lookalikes.name: Dickcissel
lookalikes.tell: Smaller, with a thick bill and a small black bib.

plumage: Males and females look alike. The yellow and black are duller in fall and winter.
seasonNote: All year across much of the West. Summer only on the northern Plains and in Canada.
nameNote: Named for its meadow home, though it isn't a lark: it's in the blackbird family. Sturnella means little starling; neglecta means overlooked, because earlier naturalists had mixed it up with the Eastern Meadowlark.

fact: Its flute-like song spirals upward, each phrase climbing higher than the last.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Dense, damp forests in summer; it migrates through woods and parks.
listen: Breezy, flute-like phrases that spiral upward.

lookalikes.name: Hermit Thrush
lookalikes.tell: A reddish tail that stands out from the back.

lookalikes.name: Veery
lookalikes.tell: Warmer reddish-brown, with faint, blurry spots.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year. Pacific Coast birds are russet, inland birds olive.
seasonNote: Passes through most of the US in May and September, migrating at night. Summers in Canadian and western mountain forests; winters in South America.
nameNote: Named for William Swainson, an English naturalist. Catharus means pure; ustulatus means scorched, for its brown color.

fact: Its song spirals downward, sounding like it is being sung inside a metal pipe.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Damp leafy forests with thick undergrowth.
listen: A breezy song that spirals downward, "veer, veer, veer."
marks: Faint, blurry spots on a buff throat

lookalikes.name: Wood Thrush
lookalikes.tell: Bold black spots all down the breast.

lookalikes.name: Swainson's Thrush
lookalikes.tell: Olive-brown, with buff spectacles.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year.
seasonNote: Summer in damp northern and eastern forests, May to August. Winters in Brazil.
nameNote: Named for its song, "veer, veer." Catharus means pure; fuscescens means darkish.

fact: It is named for its domed nest on the forest floor, shaped like an old outdoor oven.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: The floor of mature leafy forests, walking rather than hopping.
listen: "Teacher, teacher, TEACHER," getting louder as it goes.
marks: Orange crown stripe edged in black
Olive back, and dark streaks on a white breast

lookalikes.name: Northern Waterthrush
lookalikes.tell: A bold eyebrow instead of an eye-ring, no orange crown, and it bobs its tail near water.

lookalikes.name: Wood Thrush
lookalikes.tell: Much bigger, with round spots and a rusty head.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year.
seasonNote: Summer in eastern and northern forests, May to September. Winters from Mexico to the Caribbean.
nameNote: Named for its domed nest on the forest floor, shaped like an old outdoor oven. Seiurus means tail-shaker; aurocapilla means golden-haired.

fact: Its bright song is often remembered as "sweet, sweet, sweet, I'm so sweet."
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Willows, wet thickets and shrubby edges near water.
listen: Bright and quick: "sweet, sweet, sweet, I'm so sweet."
marks: Black eye on a plain yellow face

lookalikes.name: American Goldfinch
lookalikes.tell: Black wings with white bars, and a cone-shaped bill.

lookalikes.name: Wilson's Warbler
lookalikes.tell: A neat black cap on the male.

plumage: Males are bright yellow with red streaks. Females are plainer, with faint or no streaks. Young birds can be quite gray.
seasonNote: Summer across most of North America, May to August. Winters from Mexico to South America.
nameNote: Named for its color. Setophaga means moth-eater; petechia means small red spots on the skin, for the male's streaks.

fact: The masked male sings a rolling "witchety-witchety-witchety" from marshes and wet fields.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Marshes, wet fields and dense low growth.
listen: A rolling "witchety-witchety-witchety."

lookalikes.name: Kentucky Warbler
lookalikes.tell: Yellow 'spectacles' and yellow all the way down the belly.

lookalikes.name: Yellow Warbler
lookalikes.tell: No mask, and yellow all over.

plumage: Males have a black mask with a pale band above it. Females have no mask, just an olive face and a yellow throat.
seasonNote: Summer across nearly all of the US and Canada, April to October. All year along the Gulf and Pacific coasts.
nameNote: Named for its yellow throat. Geothlypis means ground finch; trichas is a Greek name for a thrush.

fact: It migrates at night and learns to steer by the stars, as experiments in a planetarium showed.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Brushy edges, roadsides and old fields, singing from wires and treetops.
listen: Bright paired notes: "what! what! where? where? see it! see it!"

lookalikes.name: Blue Grosbeak
lookalikes.tell: Bigger, with a heavy bill and rusty wing bars.

lookalikes.name: Eastern Bluebird
lookalikes.tell: An orange breast.

plumage: Males are blue in summer and turn patchy brown in fall. Females are plain warm brown. Like the Blue Jay's, the blue comes from light scattering, not pigment.
seasonNote: Summer across the East, May to September. Winters in Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, navigating by the stars at night.
nameNote: Named for its indigo blue. Passerina means sparrow-like; cyanea means blue.

fact: It used to line its nest with horsehair so often that it was nicknamed the hair bird.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Open woods, parks and lawns with scattered trees.
listen: A long, dry trill on one pitch, like a tiny sewing machine.

lookalikes.name: American Tree Sparrow
lookalikes.tell: In winter: a rusty cap plus a dark spot on the breast and a two-toned bill.

lookalikes.name: Clay-colored Sparrow
lookalikes.tell: A brown cheek patch and no black eye line.

plumage: Males and females look alike. In winter the rusty cap fades to brown and the face gets plainer.
seasonNote: Summer across most of North America, April to October. Winters in the southern US and Mexico.
nameNote: Named for its chipping call. Spizella means little finch; passerina means sparrow-like.

fact: Often called the snowbird, because it shows up at feeders across much of the US as winter arrives.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Conifer forests in summer; yards and feeders in winter, flashing white tail edges.
listen: A musical trill on one pitch, and sharp ticking calls.
marks: White outer tail feathers that flash in flight

lookalikes.name: Eastern Towhee
lookalikes.tell: Bigger, with rusty sides and red eyes.

lookalikes.name: White-crowned Sparrow
lookalikes.tell: A bold striped head.

plumage: Females are browner than males. There are several regional forms: all slate gray in the East, and the 'Oregon' form in the West with a black hood and a brown back.
seasonNote: Winter across most of the US, October to April, which is why it's called the snowbird. Summers in Canada and mountain forests.
nameNote: Junco comes from the Latin for a rush, a mix-up, since it doesn't live in reeds. Hyemalis means of winter.

fact: A male's red comes from pigments in his food, and females tend to prefer the reddest males.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Towns, farms and backyard feeders.
listen: A long, cheerful warble that often ends in a buzzy note.
marks: Brown streaks on the belly and sides
Short bill with a curved top

lookalikes.name: Purple Finch
lookalikes.tell: Raspberry color washed over the back too, and no streaks on the belly.

lookalikes.name: House Sparrow
lookalikes.tell: A gray crown and black bib, and no red.

plumage: Males are red, orange or yellow, depending on what they ate while growing new feathers. Females are plain streaky brown.
seasonNote: All year across most of the US and southern Canada. Originally a western bird; some were released in New York in 1940 and spread east.
nameNote: Named for living around houses. Haemorhous comes from the Greek for blood, for the male's red; mexicanus means from Mexico.

fact: It sings its own name, and was the first bird ever banded in North America, by Audubon in 1804.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Near water, under bridges and the eaves of buildings, wagging its tail.
listen: A raspy "fee-bee," its own name.
marks: Dark gray-brown head, darker than the back
Wags its tail down and up

lookalikes.name: Eastern Wood-Pewee
lookalikes.tell: Pale wing bars, and it doesn't wag its tail.

lookalikes.name: Eastern Kingbird
lookalikes.tell: Black above, with a white tip on the tail.

plumage: Males and females look alike. In fall, fresh feathers give the belly a yellow wash.
seasonNote: One of the first migrants back, in March. Summers across the East and Canada; winters in the Southeast and Mexico.
nameNote: Named for its call, "fee-bee." Sayornis honors the naturalist Thomas Say; phoebe repeats the call.

fact: Its song has local dialects, so birds a few miles apart can sound noticeably different.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Brushy areas and weedy fields, especially in winter.
listen: A clear whistle followed by buzzy notes and a trill, in a local dialect.

lookalikes.name: White-throated Sparrow
lookalikes.tell: A white throat and a yellow spot by the eye.

lookalikes.name: Golden-crowned Sparrow
lookalikes.tell: On the West Coast: yellow at the front of the crown.

plumage: Males and females look alike. Young birds have brown and tan head stripes instead of black and white.
seasonNote: Winter across most of the US, October to April. Summers in the Arctic and western mountains; all year on the Pacific Coast.
nameNote: Named for its white crown. Zonotrichia means banded hair; leucophrys means white eyebrow.

fact: The red on the male's face likely comes from pigments in the insects it eats.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Open conifer and mixed forests in the West.
listen: Like a hoarse American Robin, short burry phrases.
marks: Black wings with two pale wing bars

lookalikes.name: Bullock's Oriole
lookalikes.tell: An orange body, a black throat and a thin, pointed bill.

lookalikes.name: Scarlet Tanager
lookalikes.tell: In the East: a red body and black wings with no wing bars.

plumage: Males are yellow with a red head in summer; the red fades in fall. Females are olive-yellow with grayer wings.
seasonNote: Summer in western forests, May to August, and seen across western lowlands during migration. Winters in Mexico and Central America.
nameNote: Tanager comes from tangara, a Tupi word from Brazil, and Piranga is another Tupi word. Ludoviciana means from Louisiana, the old Louisiana Territory.

fact: Its call is remembered as "Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?"
size: About the size of a crow
habitat: Mature forests and wooded swamps, often near water.
listen: "Who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?"
marks: Round head with no ear tufts
Bars across the chest, streaks down the belly

lookalikes.name: Great Horned Owl
lookalikes.tell: Ear tufts and yellow eyes.

lookalikes.name: Spotted Owl
lookalikes.tell: In the West: white spots instead of bars and streaks. Barred Owls are moving into its forests.

plumage: Males and females look alike; females are bigger. Young owls are fluffy white and gray.
seasonNote: All year in the East and across Canada, and spreading into the Pacific Northwest. It doesn't migrate.
nameNote: Named for the bars on its chest. Strix means owl; varia means varied.

fact: It sings nearly all year, and near street lights it will often sing at night.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Gardens, parks and woodland, often following gardeners for worms.
listen: A wistful, liquid warbling, sung nearly all year.

lookalikes.name: Common Redstart
lookalikes.tell: Slimmer, with a rusty tail it quivers, and a black face on the male.

lookalikes.name: Eurasian Bullfinch
lookalikes.tell: A pink-red breast, black cap and thick bill.

plumage: Males and females look alike. Young birds are speckled brown with no orange.
seasonNote: All year across Britain and western Europe. Northern and eastern birds move south and west for winter.
nameNote: Robin was a pet name, as in Robin Redbreast. Erithacus is an ancient Greek name for a bird; rubecula means little red one.

fact: Its mellow, flute-like song is a classic sound of dawn and dusk, often delivered from a rooftop.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Gardens, parks and woods, singing from rooftops and treetops at dawn and dusk.
listen: Slow, mellow, flute-like phrases.

lookalikes.name: Ring Ouzel
lookalikes.tell: A white crescent across the chest.

lookalikes.name: Common Starling
lookalikes.tell: Glossy and speckled, with a shorter tail.

plumage: Males are black with a yellow bill. Females are dark brown with a faintly spotted throat. Young birds are spotty and gingery.
seasonNote: All year across most of Europe. Northern birds move south for winter.
nameNote: Blackbird for the male's color. Turdus means thrush; merula is Latin for blackbird.

fact: It repeats each phrase two or three times before moving on to the next.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Gardens, parks and woods with undergrowth.
listen: Bold phrases, each repeated two or three times.
marks: Neat dark spots in lines on a cream breast

lookalikes.name: Mistle Thrush
lookalikes.tell: Bigger and grayer, with bigger round spots and white in the tail.

lookalikes.name: Redwing
lookalikes.tell: In winter: a cream eyebrow and red sides.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year.
seasonNote: All year in Britain and western Europe. Summer only in the north and east.
nameNote: Named for its song. Turdus means thrush; philomelos means song-lover.

fact: One of the smallest birds in Europe, it packs dozens of notes into a few seconds of song.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Undergrowth, gardens and woodland, low and mouse-like.
listen: A startlingly loud, fast song packed with trills.

lookalikes.name: Dunnock
lookalikes.tell: Bigger, with a gray head, a streaky back and a tail it doesn't cock.

lookalikes.name: Eurasian Treecreeper
lookalikes.tell: Climbs tree trunks, with a white belly and a curved bill.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year.
seasonNote: All year across Europe, and one of Britain's most common birds.
nameNote: Wren comes from Old English. Troglodytes means cave-dweller, for the way it creeps into crevices.

fact: Chaffinches have regional dialects: birds a few valleys apart sing slightly different songs.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Woods, parks and gardens across Europe.
listen: A descending rattle of notes that ends in a flourish.

lookalikes.name: Brambling
lookalikes.tell: In winter: orange shoulders and breast, and a white rump.

lookalikes.name: Eurasian Bullfinch
lookalikes.tell: A black cap and no white wing bars.

plumage: Males are pink-breasted with a blue-gray cap, brightest in spring. Females are olive-brown but share the white wing bars.
seasonNote: All year across Europe. Northern birds flock south and west for winter.
nameNote: Named for picking through chaff in farmyards. Fringilla means finch; coelebs means bachelor, because males stay north in winter while many females leave.

fact: Its rich warbling earned it the nickname "northern nightingale."
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Woodland and gardens with plenty of shrubs.
listen: A rich, fluty warble that bursts out of thick cover.
marks: Neat cap, black (male) or rusty brown (female)

lookalikes.name: Marsh Tit
lookalikes.tell: A black cap and a small black bib, with white cheeks.

lookalikes.name: Garden Warbler
lookalikes.tell: Plain all over, with no cap.

plumage: Males have a black cap; females and young have a rusty-brown one.
seasonNote: Summer across Europe, April to September. More and more now winter in Britain and Ireland, flying in from Central Europe.
nameNote: Named for the male's black cap. Sylvia means woodland; atricapilla means black-haired.

fact: Where it meets the Black-capped Chickadee, the two interbreed, and the hybrids can sing either song.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Leafy woods, parks and backyards across the Southeast, often with titmice.
listen: Four clear whistled notes, "fee-bee, fee-bay," and a fast "chick-a-dee-dee."
marks: Gray wings with little white edging

lookalikes.name: Black-capped Chickadee
lookalikes.tell: More white on the wings, a ragged lower edge to the bib, and a two-note song.

lookalikes.name: Tufted Titmouse
lookalikes.tell: A gray crest and no black bib.

plumage: Males, females and young all look alike, all year.
seasonNote: All year across the Southeast, north to about New Jersey and Kansas. It doesn't migrate.
nameNote: Named for the Carolinas. Poecile is Greek for many-colored; carolinensis means from Carolina.

fact: It walks headfirst down tree trunks, finding insects that woodpeckers climbing upward miss.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Mature leafy woods, parks and backyard trees, creeping along trunks and big branches.
listen: A fast, nasal "wha-wha-wha," and a toy-horn "yank" call.
marks: Black or gray cap over a white face
Blue-gray back and a long, slightly upturned bill

lookalikes.name: Red-breasted Nuthatch
lookalikes.tell: Smaller, with a black eye stripe and a rusty breast.

lookalikes.name: Black-capped Chickadee
lookalikes.tell: A black bib, and it perches rather than creeping on bark.

plumage: Males have a black cap; females' caps are grayer. Colors stay the same all year.
seasonNote: All year across most of the US and southern Canada. It doesn't migrate.
nameNote: Nuthatch comes from nut hack, for wedging seeds in bark and hacking them open. Sitta is Greek for a nuthatch.

fact: It's North America's smallest woodpecker, and it will even climb weed stems to dig out insect larvae.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Woods, orchards, parks and backyards; often at suet feeders.
listen: A sharp "pik," a descending whinny, and soft, fast drumming on wood in spring.
marks: Black and white with a white stripe down the back
Small red patch on the back of the head (male)

lookalikes.name: Hairy Woodpecker
lookalikes.tell: Bigger, with a much longer bill, about as long as its head.

lookalikes.name: Red-bellied Woodpecker
lookalikes.tell: Barred back and a lot more red on the head.

plumage: Males have a red spot on the back of the head; females don't. Colors stay the same all year.
seasonNote: All year across most of the US and Canada. It doesn't migrate.
nameNote: Downy for the soft white feathers on its back. Dryobates means tree-walker; pubescens means downy.

fact: Its red belly is so faint it's rarely seen; the bright red is actually on its head.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Leafy woods, parks and backyards with big trees; a regular at feeders.
listen: A rolling "churr" or "kwirr," and drumming on trees and gutters.
marks: Red cap running down the back of the neck

lookalikes.name: Red-headed Woodpecker
lookalikes.tell: An all-red head, and big solid white wing patches.

lookalikes.name: Northern Flicker
lookalikes.tell: Brown with black spots, and a white rump in flight.

plumage: Males have red from the bill to the nape; females only on the nape. Young birds have no red cap.
seasonNote: All year across the eastern US, slowly spreading north. It doesn't migrate.
nameNote: Named for the faint red wash on its belly. Melanerpes means black creeper; carolinus means from Carolina.

fact: It's a woodpecker that feeds mostly on the ground, licking up ants with a long, sticky tongue.
size: Between a robin and a crow
habitat: Open woods, parks and lawns, often hopping on the ground.
listen: A loud, long "wick-wick-wick-wick," and a single "kleer!" call.
marks: Brown, with black spots below and a black crescent on the chest
White rump that flashes in flight
Yellow (East) or salmon-red (West) under the wings

lookalikes.name: Red-bellied Woodpecker
lookalikes.tell: Black-and-white barred back and a red cap.

lookalikes.name: Mourning Dove
lookalikes.tell: A plain body with no spots on the breast, a small head and a long pointed tail.

plumage: Males have a mustache stripe, black in the East and red in the West; females don't.
seasonNote: All year across most of the US. Summer only in Canada and the far North.
nameNote: Flicker may come from its call, or the flicker of its wings. Colaptes means chiseler; auratus means golden, for the eastern birds' wings.

fact: Flocks sometimes pass a single berry beak to beak down a row of birds on a branch.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Orchards, woodland edges and berry trees, in roving flocks.
listen: Very high, thin whistles, "sreee," with no real song.
marks: Soft brown crest and black mask
Red waxy tips on the wing feathers

lookalikes.name: Bohemian Waxwing
lookalikes.tell: Grayer, with rusty feathers under the tail and white and yellow on the wings.

plumage: Males and females look alike. Young birds are streaky and paler.
seasonNote: Wanders all year, following berries. Common in the North in summer and the South in winter.
nameNote: Named for the red, wax-like tips on its wings. Bombycilla means silk-tail; cedrorum means of cedars, for the berries it eats.

fact: Crows recognize individual human faces and can remember someone who bothered them for years.
size: About the size of a crow
habitat: Almost anywhere: fields, towns, parks, roadsides and beaches.
listen: A loud, harsh "caw-caw-caw," plus rattles, clicks and soft chatter.

lookalikes.name: Common Raven
lookalikes.tell: Much bigger, with a wedge-shaped tail, shaggy throat and deep croak.

lookalikes.name: Common Grackle
lookalikes.tell: Much smaller and slimmer, with pale eyes and a long tail.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year. Young birds stay with the family and help raise the next brood.
seasonNote: All year across most of the US. Northern birds move south and gather in huge winter roosts.
nameNote: Crow comes from Old English, after its call. Corvus means crow; brachyrhynchos means short-billed.

fact: It sometimes sits on an anthill and lets ants crawl through its feathers, which may clear out mites.
size: Between a robin and a crow
habitat: Lawns, fields, marshes and towns, in noisy flocks.
listen: A creaky, rusty-hinge squeak, "readle-eak," and a sharp "chuck."

lookalikes.name: Red-winged Blackbird
lookalikes.tell: Smaller, with a short tail and red shoulders.

lookalikes.name: American Crow
lookalikes.tell: Much bigger, with dark eyes and a short tail.

plumage: Males are glossy and long-tailed; females are smaller and browner. Young birds have dark eyes.
seasonNote: All year in the Southeast. Summer only in the North and on the Plains, arriving in early spring.
nameNote: Grackle comes from the Latin graculus, a jackdaw. Quiscalus quiscula is a Latinized version of a local name.

fact: A male may know a hundred variations of its song and sing them from the same fence post all morning.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Grasslands, hayfields and pastures in the East.
listen: Clear, slurred whistles, "see-you, see-yeeer," sweet and simple.
marks: White outer tail feathers in flight

lookalikes.name: Western Meadowlark
lookalikes.tell: Nearly identical; its song is a longer, bubbling, flute-like tumble.

lookalikes.name: Dickcissel
lookalikes.tell: Smaller, with a thick bill and a small black bib.

plumage: Males and females look alike; the colors are duller in fall and winter.
seasonNote: All year across much of the East and South. Summer only in the North.
nameNote: Named for its meadow home, though it's a blackbird, not a lark. Sturnella means little starling; magna means big.

fact: Despite the male's blazing red, it's hard to spot, because it stays high in the leafy canopy.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: High in mature leafy forests, especially oaks, in summer.
listen: Like a robin with a sore throat: short, burry phrases, and a "chick-burr" call.

lookalikes.name: Northern Cardinal
lookalikes.tell: A crest, a black face and a red bill, and red wings too.

lookalikes.name: Summer Tanager
lookalikes.tell: Red all over, including the wings.

plumage: Males are scarlet with black wings in summer and turn olive-green in fall. Females are olive-yellow all year.
seasonNote: Summer in eastern forests, May to August. Winters in South America.
nameNote: Tanager comes from tangara, a Tupi word from Brazil. Olivacea means olive, for the female and the fall male.

fact: Roger Tory Peterson described it as a sparrow dipped in raspberry juice.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Conifer and mixed forests; feeders in winter.
listen: A fast, rich, rolling warble, and a sharp "pik" in flight.
marks: Raspberry red head, breast and back (male)
No brown streaks on the belly
Female has a bold white eyebrow

lookalikes.name: House Finch
lookalikes.tell: Brown streaks on the belly and sides, and red mostly on the head and breast.

plumage: Males are raspberry red. Females are brown and white with bold face stripes. Young males look like females for a year.
seasonNote: All year in the Northeast and on the Pacific Coast. Winter only across much of the East.
nameNote: Named for the male's purple-red color. Haemorhous comes from the Greek for blood; purpureus means purple.

fact: It weighs about as much as a penny, yet flies nonstop across the Gulf of Mexico each spring.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Gardens, woodland edges and feeders, around tube-shaped flowers.
listen: No song: just high squeaks, chips and the hum of its wings.
marks: Tiny, with a long needle bill

lookalikes.name: Black-chinned Hummingbird
lookalikes.tell: In the West: the male's throat is black with a purple band.

plumage: Males have a ruby throat that looks black in the shade. Females have a white throat.
seasonNote: Summer across the East, April to September. Winters in Central America.
nameNote: Named for the male's ruby throat. Archilochus was an ancient Greek poet; colubris is an old word for hummingbird.

fact: To lure danger from its nest, it limps away dragging a wing as if it's broken.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Lawns, fields, parking lots, gravel roofs and shorelines.
listen: A shrill, repeated "kill-deer, kill-deer," often at night.
marks: Two black bands across a white chest

lookalikes.name: Semipalmated Plover
lookalikes.tell: Smaller, with one chest band and a stubby orange bill.

plumage: Males and females look alike. Chicks have one chest band and can run within hours of hatching.
seasonNote: All year across most of the US. Summer only in the North, arriving in early spring.
nameNote: Named for its call. Charadrius is Greek for a plover; vociferus means noisy.

fact: It nests in the dead of winter, so its owlets are ready to hunt by late summer.
size: About the size of a crow
habitat: Woods, deserts, farmland, parks and suburbs, nearly anywhere with trees.
listen: Deep, soft hoots in a rhythm: "hoo-h'HOO, hoo, hoo."

lookalikes.name: Barred Owl
lookalikes.tell: No ear tufts and dark brown eyes.

lookalikes.name: Long-eared Owl
lookalikes.tell: Much slimmer, with tufts set close together and a rusty face.

plumage: Males and females look alike; females are bigger, but males hoot deeper.
seasonNote: All year across almost all of North America. It doesn't migrate.
nameNote: Named for its feather tufts, which aren't ears or horns. Bubo means owl; virginianus means from Virginia.

fact: It keeps singing through the hot middle of the day, long after most birds have gone quiet.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Leafy woods and shade trees, sallying out from a dead branch to catch insects.
listen: A slow, sweet, sliding whistle, "pee-a-wee," then a falling "pee-yer."
marks: Gray-olive with two pale wing bars
Dark vest on the sides of the breast

lookalikes.name: Eastern Phoebe
lookalikes.tell: No wing bars, and it wags its tail.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year.
seasonNote: Summer across the East, May to September. Winters in South America.
nameNote: Named for its song. Contopus means short-footed; virens means green.

fact: It fearlessly attacks crows and hawks many times its size that fly near its nest.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Open fields, roadsides and lake edges, on wires and fence posts.
listen: Sharp, electric, sputtering "kit-kit-kitter" calls.
marks: White tip on a black tail

lookalikes.name: Eastern Phoebe
lookalikes.tell: Smaller and browner, with no white tip on the tail.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year.
seasonNote: Summer across most of North America, May to August. Winters in the Amazon, where it eats mostly fruit.
nameNote: Kingbird for how it bosses other birds. Tyrannus tyrannus means tyrant, twice.

fact: It scratches for food with a two-footed backward hop, kicking leaves behind it.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Brushy hillsides, thickets and overgrown gardens in the West.
listen: A buzzy trill, sometimes with a few notes first, and a cat-like "mew" call.
marks: Black hood and back, with white spots on the wings and back

lookalikes.name: Eastern Towhee
lookalikes.tell: No white spots on the back.

lookalikes.name: American Robin
lookalikes.tell: Orange across the whole breast, and no black hood.

plumage: Males are black above; females are dark brown. Young birds are streaky.
seasonNote: All year across much of the West. Summer only on the northern Plains.
nameNote: Towhee is named for a call of its eastern cousin. Pipilo means I chirp; maculatus means spotted.

fact: It can imitate hawks, squirrels, cats and even dogs.
size: Between a robin and a crow
habitat: Conifer forests, mountain campgrounds and western backyards.
listen: Harsh "shack-shack-shack" calls, and good hawk imitations.

lookalikes.name: Blue Jay
lookalikes.tell: In the East: white on the wings and face, and a black necklace.

lookalikes.name: California Scrub-Jay
lookalikes.tell: No crest, and a white throat.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year.
seasonNote: All year in western forests, from Alaska to Central America. Some move downhill in winter.
nameNote: Named for Georg Steller, a German naturalist who saw it in Alaska in 1741. Cyanocitta is Greek for blue jay.

fact: Both parents sing to each other while taking turns sitting on the eggs.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Leafy and mixed woods, streamsides and gardens in the West.
listen: A rich, rising and falling warble, like a robin that took singing lessons.
marks: Huge pale bill and white wing patches

lookalikes.name: Rose-breasted Grosbeak
lookalikes.tell: In the East: the male is white below, with a rose chest.

lookalikes.name: Spotted Towhee
lookalikes.tell: A thin bill, red eyes and white spots on the back.

plumage: Males are black and orange. Females are brown with a buffy breast and a bold white eyebrow.
seasonNote: Summer in the West, May to August. Winters in Mexico.
nameNote: Grosbeak means big beak. Pheucticus means shy; melanocephalus means black-headed.

fact: It has lived alongside people for at least 10,000 years and is now found on every continent except Antarctica.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Towns, farms and city streets, almost always near buildings.
listen: Endless cheerful chirps, "cheep, cheep," from roofs and hedges.
marks: Chestnut on the sides of the head
Plain buff female with a pale eye stripe

lookalikes.name: House Finch
lookalikes.tell: Streaky, with red on the male's head and no black bib.

lookalikes.name: Song Sparrow
lookalikes.tell: Heavy streaks on the breast and a long tail.

plumage: Males have a gray cap, black bib and chestnut nape; the bib is bigger and blacker in spring. Females are plain buff-brown.
seasonNote: All year wherever there are people. It doesn't migrate.
nameNote: Named for living around houses. Passer is Latin for sparrow; domesticus means of the house.

fact: All of North America's 80 million or so starlings come from about 100 birds released in New York in 1890.
size: About the size of a robin
habitat: Towns, lawns and farmland, in big, swirling flocks.
listen: A long jumble of whistles, clicks and rattles, with imitations of other birds and car alarms.
marks: Glossy black with purple and green sheen
White spots in winter; short, square tail

lookalikes.name: Common Grackle
lookalikes.tell: A long tail and pale eyes.

lookalikes.name: Common Blackbird
lookalikes.tell: A longer tail and no glossy sheen.

plumage: Males and females look alike. New feathers in fall have white tips, so starlings look spotted in winter, then wear to glossy black by spring.
seasonNote: All year across North America and Europe; northern birds move south for winter.
nameNote: Starling comes from Old English for little star, maybe for the winter spots. Sturnus vulgaris means common starling.

fact: Some great tits learned to peck through the foil tops of milk bottles left on doorsteps.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Woods, parks and gardens across Europe; a regular at feeders.
listen: A loud, ringing "tea-cher, tea-cher," plus dozens of other calls.
marks: Glossy black head with white cheeks
Yellow breast with a black stripe down the middle

lookalikes.name: Eurasian Blue Tit
lookalikes.tell: Smaller, with a blue cap and no black stripe down the breast.

lookalikes.name: Coal Tit
lookalikes.tell: Smaller, with a white patch on the nape and no yellow.

plumage: Males have a wide black breast stripe; females' is thinner. Young birds have yellowish cheeks.
seasonNote: All year across Europe. It doesn't migrate.
nameNote: Tit is an old word for a small bird. Parus means titmouse; major means bigger.

fact: Its blue cap reflects ultraviolet light, which other blue tits can see and people can't.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Woods, parks and gardens; often hanging upside down on feeders.
listen: A bright "tsee-tsee-tsu-hu-hu-hu" and a scolding churr.
marks: White face with a dark eye stripe

lookalikes.name: Great Tit
lookalikes.tell: Bigger, with a black head and a black stripe down the breast.

plumage: Males and females look alike, though males are a little brighter. Young birds are washed yellow.
seasonNote: All year across Europe. It doesn't migrate.
nameNote: Named for its blue cap. Cyanistes and caeruleus both mean blue.

fact: It looks plain, but its family life is complicated: females often pair with two males at once.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Hedges, gardens and scrub, shuffling on the ground under bushes.
listen: A fast, squeaky warble, a bit like a wren's song but slower and flatter.

lookalikes.name: House Sparrow
lookalikes.tell: A thick cone bill and no blue-gray.

lookalikes.name: Eurasian Wren
lookalikes.tell: Tiny, all brown, with its tail cocked up.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year.
seasonNote: All year across western Europe. Summer only in the north and east.
nameNote: Dunnock means little dun (brown) one. Prunella means little brown; modularis means singing.

fact: It has been painted into hundreds of Renaissance paintings, often in the hand of the infant Jesus.
size: Smaller than a sparrow
habitat: Gardens, weedy fields and parks, feeding on thistle and teasel heads.
listen: A liquid, tinkling twitter, often from a flock.
marks: Bright yellow bar across black wings

lookalikes.name: Common Chaffinch
lookalikes.tell: Pink breast, white wing bars and no red face.

plumage: Males and females look nearly alike. Young birds have no red face and a plain gray-brown head.
seasonNote: All year across most of Europe. Northern birds move south for winter.
nameNote: Named for the gold in its wings. Carduelis comes from carduus, Latin for thistle.

fact: Males sing through the night mainly to attract a mate; once paired, many sing mostly at dawn.
size: About the size of a sparrow
habitat: Dense thickets, scrub and woodland undergrowth in southern and western Europe.
listen: Loud, rich and varied: pure whistles, rich chuckles and a crescendo of "pew-pew-pew."

lookalikes.name: Common Redstart
lookalikes.tell: A rusty tail it quivers, and the male has a black face.

lookalikes.name: Garden Warbler
lookalikes.tell: Plainer, grayer, and no rusty tail.

plumage: Males and females look alike. Young birds are spotted.
seasonNote: Summer in southern and western Europe, April to August. Winters in tropical Africa.
nameNote: Nightingale means night singer in Old English. Luscinia is Latin for nightingale; megarhynchos means big-billed.

fact: It sings while rising almost straight up, hovering so high it's hard to see, sometimes for ten minutes.
size: Between a sparrow and a robin
habitat: Open farmland, meadows, moors and dunes.
listen: A long, unbroken stream of trills and warbles poured out from high in the sky.
marks: White edges to the tail and wings in flight

lookalikes.name: Meadow Pipit
lookalikes.tell: Slimmer, with a thin bill and no crest.

plumage: Males and females look alike all year.
seasonNote: All year in Britain and western Europe. Summer only in the north and east.
nameNote: Named for singing high in the sky. Alauda is Latin for lark; arvensis means of the fields.
